content.title: About
content.content: Broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. italica) is a green vegetable with a thick, edible stalk topped by tightly packed flower buds called florets. It belongs to the cabbage family and was developed in the Mediterranean region, particularly Italy. Broccoli has a mild, slightly bitter, fresh flavor and is eaten raw or cooked.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Broccoli belongs to the same species as cabbage, cauliflower, kale, and Brussels sprouts.
The name comes from the Italian word broccolo, meaning the flowering top of a cabbage.
The florets are the vegetable's immature flower buds.
Chopping or chewing broccoli helps form sulforaphane, a compound that is being studied for its biological activity.
The stalk and leaves of broccoli are also edible.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C and vitamin K
items.content: Broccoli is an excellent source of vitamin C, which supports the immune system, and vitamin K, which supports blood clotting and bones.

items.title: Provides folate and potassium
items.content: These nutrients support cell function and normal blood pressure.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Broccoli contributes fiber that supports normal digestion.

items.title: Contains glucosinolates
items.content: Compounds in broccoli, including those that form sulforaphane, have shown antioxidant and protective activity in laboratory studies.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Broccoli is low in calories and filling, making it a nutrient-dense choice.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Broccoli can cause gas or bloating in sensitive individuals, especially when eaten raw or in large amounts.

items.title: Thyroid considerations
items.content: Cruciferous vegetables contain compounds that may affect thyroid function in very large amounts. People with thyroid conditions should consult a healthcare professional.

items.title: Possible medication interactions
items.content: Broccoli contains vitamin K. People taking blood thinners should consult a healthcare professional about keeping their intake consistent.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Broccoli allergy is uncommon but can occur.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Broccoli can be eaten raw in salads or with dips, or steamed, roasted, stir-fried, boiled, or added to soups, casseroles, and pasta. Light steaming or quick cooking helps preserve its color, texture, and nutrients. The stalk can be peeled and sliced for cooking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unwashed broccoli in the refrigerator in a perforated bag, where it usually keeps for about a week. Wash it right before use. Broccoli can also be blanched and frozen. Avoid heads that are turning yellow or smell sulfurous.
